Negroes Were Determined to Protect One of Their Race From Lynching.

WINSTON, N. C., Aug. 12.—A serious riot between whites and blacks was narrowly averted here last night. It was given out in colored churches during the day that an attempt was going to be made to lynch Arthur Tuttle, a negro on trial here for the mnrder of Policeman Vickers last May.

After church about 150 negroes organized and marched to the jail where they remained for several hours. They were armed with pistols and guns. Mayor Gray went to the jail and assured the negroes that there was no danger of lynching and begged them to disperse. Sheriff McArthur and two lawyers also addressed the negroes assuring then there was no danger of lynching. Judge Brown who is holding court, notified the negroes that they were violating the law, telling them that Tuttle should have a fair trail and that he would be responsible for Tuttle's protection. The negroes said they would leave if the sheriff would put a guard of 20 men around the jail: This was done, but many of the mob refused to go away.

Sheriff McArthur then ordered out the Forsythe riflemen, besides a number of deputies, who were sworn in. Judge Brown also instructed the sheriff to arrest those who did not leave. The mob began firing on the officers, several of whom were struck with small bird shot, but none seriously wounded.

The riflemen fired several volleys into the crowd, causing the negroes to disperse in quick order. Fourteen of the rioters were arrested by the officers and put in jail.

Everything was quiet at 10 o'clock this morning.

The News on the Train.

On the train coming from Greensboro yesterday the riot was the subject discussed by all the passengers. One gentleman stated that the negroes were aroused by a number of people returning from the Friends meeting at High Point. It was after midnight when they rode through the town. The negroes thought that it was a mob forming to lynch Tuttle, and they gathered around the jail in large numbers. Judge Brown gave orders, so the story went, to the sheriff to call out the military summon sufficient deputies and if within a given time the mob had not dispersed to open fire. Later on Mayor Eugene Gray coming upon the scene rescinded the Judge's orders and after assuring the negroes that no violence to Tuttle was contemplated or would be tolerated, ordered everybody to disperse. RALEIGH, N. C., August 12.—(Special.)—The Adjutant-General to-day received telegrams from Winston, from Captain J. C. Bessent, commanding the local military, informing him of the action of the negro mob there last night.

RIOT IN WINSTON.
Authur Tuttle, the colored man who killed policeman Vickers in Winston last May, has been on trial for his life in Winston. Sunday night a company of Friends who had been attending their annual meeting at High Point, passed through Winston returning home. The colored people became alarmed and thought it was a band going to the jail to lynch Tuttle. They soon gathered around the jail in large numbers. Custom, in its usmal form, has practically become law in this country, insomuch that when a man digresses from it, he is rebuked either in secret or openly.

The ridiculous attempt of an armed body of white men in North Carolina last week, to lynch a colored man, failed by the co-operation of colored men stoutly resisting, in which a few men on either side were shot, but not seriously injured. THE RIOTERS IN JAIL
FIFTY NEGROES UNDER ARREST FOR SUNDAY NIGHT'S TROUBLE.
TRUE BILLS AGAINST 50 OTHERS.
A crowd collected in West Winston Wednesday Night, but dispersed before the Officers Arrived--The Gatling Gun Still on Guard--Tuttle Gets 25 Years in the Penitentiary.

Special to the News and Observer.

WINSTON, N. C., Aug. 15.

A negro created great excitement in West Winston late last night by attempting to break in the residence of Dr. R. H. Jones. A crowd of fifty negroes were seen congregated in the woods at midnight but before officers arrived they had skipped. A suspicious negro who was armed was arrested and jailed. The Gatling gun is still here. It is not definitely known when it will be returned home.

Fifty negroes who participated in Sunday night's riot are in jail. The grand jury has returned over 100 true bills against parties connected with the trouble. It is estimated that more than two hundred negroes have left Winston since the riot.

Arthur Tuttle, the negro who shot and killed policeman Vickers here last May, gets 25 years in the penitentiary. Sentence was passed this afternoon. Counsel for defence made no motion for new trial. On his return to jail the prisoner said he was displeased with the verdict of the jury; that counsel for the State did not put the officer whom he struck the evening he shot officer Vickers on the witness stand. Tuttle referred to Policeman Hasting who was acquitted at the last term of court for killing his (Tuttle's) brother. His statement was convincing that the negro wanted to kill Mr. Hasting when he shot Vickers.

The case of Bud Cunningham for the murder of his sweetheart, last May was given to the jury to-night. A verdict of manslaughter is expected.

Albert Allred woolen, corn and wheat mills near Mt. Airy were destroyed by fire yesterday. The fire originated in the picking room from a hot box and everything was destroyed, including building, machinery, manufactured stock and 25,000 pounds of custom wool. The loss is $25,000, with no insurance.

Edward Spach, one of Winston's popular citizens, aged 82 years, in attempting to get off a moving street car late last night, was thrown violently on the street and sustained injuries which it is feared will prove fatal.

R. M. Austin, a prominent citizen of Mocksville, dropped dead while eating dinner yesterday; aged 65 years.

Dr. W. S. Taylor, of Mt. Airy, went to Patrick county, Va., to day to attend to smallpox patients.

TRIAL OF THE RIOTERS.
COUNTY AND CITY OFFICIALS TESTIFY FOR THE STATE.
The Commonwealth Trying to Prove That There Was an Unlawful Assembly. Patrick Small-Pox Cases.
WINSTON, N. C., Aug. 17.—Special.—
In the trial of Sunday night's rioters the State is represented by four able lawyers, besides the solicitor. Several prisoners have employed counsel, but many of them have none. Among witnesses examined for the State to-day were Mayor Gray, Sheriff McArthur, and Lawyer B. B. Watson, who gave damaging testimony. The State sought to establish by these witnesses the fact that there was an unlawful assemble. Several of the prisoners were identified as being present at different periods of the trouble. Some of them displayed pistols and guns. It was shown by the witnesses that the stubbornness manifested by the mob was remarkably foolish, in refusing to disperse, after the conservative warnings and the assurances given them by officials and well-known citizens.
Their folly was emphasized by a fact brought out in Mayor Gray's testimony. He was told that the negroes feared that Tuttle would be lynched by people from the country, and that they had been informed that a lot of horses were tied in the pine woods in the West End, whereupon the Mayor sent the Chief of Police with one of the negroes to the West End in order that they might be satisfied that the report was untrue. Even after this the mob persistently refused to disperse.
Governor Carr this afternoon having ordered a special term of court for the trial of the rioters, all of the cases will be disposed of next week.
It was learned to-day that Martinsville has raised her quarantine, recently instituted against the small-pox district in Patrick county. There have been no new cases for several days, and the physicians say the disease is perfectly under their control.
In the report of the grand jury to-day a strong recommendation was made for the county building a new court-house. In calling attention to the report, Judge Brown announced that the County Commissioners could build one without a vote of the people, and it was their duty to have it constructed.

WINSTON, N. C., Aug. 19.

The special term of court, ordered by Gov. Carr for the trial of Winston's negro rioters, opened today. By general consent, the jurors who heard the testimony in the case of the State against Micajah Watts and others, as far as it had proceeded during the last term, which closed Saturday, were impanelled to hear the case, and instead of recalling the witnesses the stenographic report of the evidence was read to the jury.

Counsel for four of the rioters plead guilty for his clients. Two others acknowledged their guilt.

During the examination this morning the fact was brought out that on the night of the trouble, Bob Tuttle (the brother of the man who was then on trial for the murder of Officer Vickers) went to the M. E. colored church, and just after service arose near the pulpit and stated that he learned that people from the country were coming that night to lynch his brother, and called upon those present for assistance.

It is thought to-night the trial of the rioters will be concluded Wednesday. Another of the negro rioters, who was shot, is dead.

Judge Brown Saturday night changed the sentence of Bud Cunningham from twenty to fifteen years in the penitentiary. The prisoner killed his sweetheart, but many believe he did it accidentally.

Several of Winston's tobacco manufacturers say they are short on hands to work the weed. This is occasioned by the many negroes leaving here on account of the recent riot. Many of them did not wait to get what money was due them.

Several of Winston's prominent young men were arraigned in the Superior Court here a few days ago for gambling. They all submitted, and most of them were fined $15 and cost. His Honor said that he wanted it understood if there were any more cases against these persons at the next term he would make the punishment imprisonment.

News was received here yesterday of a bad wreck which occurred Sunday evening on the Southern road near Blacksburg, S. C. The train, it appears, jumped the track. The express messenger was the only one killed. Many cars were badly damaged.

Mr. Louis M. Swink, one of Winston's rising young lawyers, will be united in marriage on September 3rd. Miss May Dreher, of Mount Pleasant, is to be his bride.

Old Moravian Home Church.

The old Moravian Home Church in Salem, which has been closed several week, undergoing a thorough renovation, was finally re opened yesterday with the annual celebration of the 13th of August service. The attendance morning and evening was large. This "house of worship" is one of the landmarks of this section. The term "Home" is used to distinguish it from the half dozen other Moravian Churches in and near Winston-Salem.

Just as the present century was being ushered in the inhabitants of the little village of Salem built the church edifice which stands at the north east point of the Salem square.

The exterior of the church is about the same as when it was built in 1800. The same clear-toned bell is heard striking the hours and calling the people to worship. The same organ is also used, built in that distant early day. Within the church, however, many changes have been made since the war. The church was handsomely frescoed about 15 years ago by Philadelphia artists, but the last renovation surpasses by far any work done heretotore. The prevailing color is light cream, two shades from white. The ceiling has a large oval center, encircled by a large rustic, laurel-leaf moulding, shaded in bold relief. The oval opening is shaded with a light cloud effect. Just outside the opening is formed a large panel, the back-ground of which is finished in fine gold lines, style Louis XIV, and on the surface at the four corners of the panel are large Italian Renaissance scroll ornaments, shaded in bold relief, and in light stucco color. WINSTON-SALEM, N. C., Sept. 3.
Winston shipped 1,147,755 pounds of manufactured tobacco during August, an increase of 340,443 pounds over the same month last year. The stamp sales for last month were $68,865 32, an increase of $20,426.56, over the same month last year. The sales of leaf tobacco on the Winston market during August aggregated 430,816 pounds, a decrease of 581,588 pounds below August, 1894.

The Winston graded schools opened yesterday with flattering prospects for a very large attendance. Over 600 pupils were enrolled. The opening exercises were held in the chapel of the West Winston school and an appropriate address was delivered by Mr. J. C. Buxton, Chairman of the School Committee.

The negro, Dave Koontz, who was injured in Winston's recent riot, was brought back from High Point yesterday and is now in jail. He has one finger shot off, besides a bad wound in the leg. He says he did not participate in the riot but was only there as a spectator.

Mr. Pedro A. Anderson arrived here yesterday from South America with two daughters and two sons. The former will attend the Salem Academy, and the latter the Davis school.

Mr. C. H. B. Leonard and Miss Bessie Jones, of Davidson county, were united in marriage last Sunday at the home of Esquire Beard, near Midway. Many of Winston's and Salem's business men are interested in the Roanoke & Southern Railroad between Winston and Roanoke, Va. Many are now of the opinion that the Norfolk & Western, which leased the road several years ago, will give it up by the non-payment of interest due on the bonds. It looks now like the Baltimore & Ohio will get control of the road.

Micajah Watts, colored, who was one of the leaders in Winston's recent riot, and who was sentenced to six months on the county roads, declined to work a few days ago when the superintendent had him severely whipped. The negro is now working without a murmur.

A farmer and his wife, living a few miles northwest of Winston, came near losing their lives last Saturday evening in their attempt to cross a swollen stream in a buggy. The vehicle was not pulled out of the stream until Sunday.

ALL IS QUIET AT BROOKSIDE

Rumors of a Threatened Attack Prove Unfounded.

WOMEN'S DISAPPEARANCE

Caused Uneasiness for a Time—A Strong Force of Deputies on Guard.
Everything has quieted down at Brookside, where the battle occurred Tuesday night between officers and negroes, and further trouble is not expected, though as a precaution several deputy sheriffs were kept on guard there last night.

For a while last night rumors of a threatened attack by the negroes floated around camp, but they were not well founded. The most suspicious circumstance was the fact that all the negro women living in the vicinity of Tuesday night's fight had gone across the creek, where they remained during the night. The negro quarters where Deputy Sheriff Wood was killed is located only a short distance from the company's office and the Southern railroad depot, and the fact that all the women had gone away from there tended to confirm the reports of threatened trouble.

A telephone message from Brookside to the Age-Herald at 10 o'clock stated that everything was quiet and that the fears of trouble which prevailed during the early part of the evening had about subsided. To quell any disturbance that might arise, however, a strong posse of deputies was kept on the ground all night.
The Age-Herald of yesterday stated that about a dozen negroes believed to have been implicated in the fight had been arrested. Sheriff Morrow investigated the matter and discharged three or four of them. The others, eight in number, were brought to the city on the Southern train at 5:15 yesterday morning and lodged in the county jail. One of these eight, Gardiner, it is claimed by the officers, fired one of the shots that killed Deputy Sheriff Wood. Two or three eye witnesses state that they saw him shoot Wood.

Another one of the prisoners is Charlie Jenkins, a brother to the one who had the quarrel with Boss Driver Harris, which was the cause of the fight. There are witnesses who claim to have seen him shooting at the officers. George Hill is another prisoner against whom good evidence is said to have been obtained. Baxter and Harris, who were with Wood at the time the latter was killed, say they saw Hill shooting at them.

Jim Bridges was arrested yesterday morning early. He is said to have been one of the leaders of the attacking party. The officers had one other of the leaders spotted last night and believed they would catch him before morning.

Deputy Sheriffs Henry Cole and Tom Jones were left at Brookside by Sheriff Morrow yesterday morning to assist in apprehending the parties connected with the fight. The balance of the posse returned to the city with Sheriff Morrow, bringing with them the eight prisoners.

The Age-Herald was informed by telephone message last night that one negro, badly wounded, had been found during the afternoon and that others who had succeeded in escaping were believed to have been shot.

The report that two or three dead bodies had been found was still in circulation last night, but no one who knew anything about it could be found. The report was, therefore, discredited.

When the Age-Herald reporter left Brookside yesterday morning Baxter, who received a flesh wound in the leg, was suffering intensely with his wound. Dr. Sholl, who had been called to see Mrs. Wood, administered opiates and emetics, and after a short time she got easier and at last reports was resting well.

While waiting at the depot for the train McClellan, a nephew of the dead officer, attempted to shoot Gardiner, the negro who is said to have killed Wood, but was prevented by officers. McClellan was devoted to his uncle and his grief at his untimely death was almost unbearable.
Deputy Sheriff Wood's remains will be brought to the city this morning and interred at the Woodlawn cemetery sometime today. His sister, Mrs. McClellan of Talladega, and his daughter who had been visiting in Anniston, came over yesterday and went on to Brookside in the afternoon. The dead officer was one of the bravest men that ever held a commission and was well liked by everybody. He came to Birmingham from Talladega a few years ago, at the expiration of his term as sheriff of that county. For two or three years he was one of the best men on the Birmingham police force.

A BLOODY Y RACE RIOT
TWO OFFICERS AND THREE NEGROES KILLED IN A PITCHED BATTLE.
OVER 100 SHOTS WERE FIRED.
An Attempt to Arrest a Discharged Driver at a Mining Camp in Alabama Results in a War Between the Whites and Blacks--Negroes Entrench Themselves in a Ditch and Pour Forth a Murderous Fire--Negroes Rescued After Ropes Were About Their Necks.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., July 31. —The Sheriff's posse returned from Brookside, the scene of last night's race riot, to day, bringing with them ten negro rioters who had been arrested, two having been rescued from the enraged white miners after ropes had been placed about their necks, preparatory to hanging them. Half a dozen officers were left at Brookside to arrest other rioters and prevent further trouble.

Investigation showed that the negroes whom deputies Woods and Baxter went to arrest were entrenched in a ditch, strongly reinforced, and poured a murderous fire out from their cover, shooting down two officers at the first volley. Reinforcements came to the whites but the negroes never ceased firing until their ammunition was exhausted. Then they fled to the woods, the whites in pursuit.

Three dead negroes are reported found and one wounded. One woman is among the rioters arrested. Half a dozen women took part in the riot. All is quiet now, but a single pistol shot would precipitate more serious trouble. All possible ammunition has been centered at Brookside in case of another attack.

The scene of the riot is a mining camp, Brookside, twenty miles from Birmingham. Yesterday Mine Boss Culverhouse, of the Sloss Iron and Steel Company, discharged a negro driver in the mines named Jim Smith. Culverhouse and Smith had a dispute and the former ordered the latter to vacate the house he occupied.

Smith refused to obey these orders and Deputy Sheriff A. T. Wood was called upon to arrest him for trespassing. Wood swore in Joel Baxter, a citizen, as a special deputy sheriff, and last night the two went to arrest Smith.

The latter had evidently been expecting them and was prepared. He had a Winchester rifle and fired at the officers as they approached. Wood was shot through the head and heart and instantly killed. Baxter received a wound which caused death soon afterward.

A number of citizens took the part of the officers and a number of negroes joined Smith. The result was a pitched battle between the races. Over 100 shots were fired with the above result. The fighting lasted over an hour.

Bitter feeling has long existed between the whites and the negro miners at Brookside and it only required such a tragedy as occurred when Deputies Woods and Baxter were killed to night to kindle the feudal flame.

The sheriff's posse reached Brookside at 1 o'clock this morning. They found that two officers and three negroes had been killed. The bodies of the latter lay in the woods, where they had fallen.

Will Albert and Charles Jenkins, colored, had just been captured by the white miners who had placed ropes about the negroes' necks and were about to string them up when the officers rescued them.

RESULT OF NEGRO RIOT.
Three Bodies Found and Others Believed to Have Been Shot.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., July 31.—It is impossible to tell how many negroes were killed in last night's race riot at Brookside. Most of the sheriff's posse that went from here have returned. They report that half a dozen negroes were seen to fall, and three bodies were found in the woods. Bob Simms, another negro rioter, was found dying in a cabin, to-day, from a wound in the side. It is believed that other wounded negroes were taken away by their companions. Eleven negro rioters were brought here and placed in jail, and officers are hunting for twelve others.

Princeton, Ill., Aug. 4.—The Italians of Spring Valley broke out to-day in a war upon the negroes, with a view of either massacring them or driving them out of the city limits.

The following negroes were seriously injured: Granville Lewis, aged forty-five, shot in head and clubbed with rifles, and face and neck badly lacerated, may die; Clement L. Martin, aged thirty-two, shot in back of the head with rifle ball, thirty buckshot in back and shoulders, seriously injured; Norman Bird, aged thirty-eight, shot in neck and head, badly bruised, internal injuries; Mrs. Bird, aged thirty-one, wife of Norman, shot in right cheek and arm, Maria Bird, daughter of Norman, aged fourteen, shot in breast; William Lee, aged thirty-four, kicked and trampled upon; Jube Sterritt, aged forty-seven, trampled upon, face lacerated and injured internally, badly cut by barbed wire fence in attempting escape from the mob; Oscar Prim, head bruised with rocks and stones; Silas Burken, bruised with clubs and shot at about thirty times; Jude Stuart, bad wound in the head from club; "Jim" Kelley, aged twenty-six, flesh wounds and clothing riddled with shot; "Will" Beck, aged thirty, badly bruised and internal injuries; Frank Turner, aged sixty-eight, shot twice in back of head and struck in back and shoulders by about forty buckshot; Frank Burns, head badly bruised, trampled upon and internal injuries.

The Italians for many months have wished to drive the negroes out of the coal mining belt, and to-day a plausible excuse for so doing presented itself. At 1 o'clock this morning an Italian was waylaid on the public highway by four negroes and robbed and shot four times, from the effects of which his physicians say he cannot live until morning. A mass-meeting of the Italians was called, and at 10 o'clock a mob of over three hundred gathered and started out for the negro village, which is two miles west of Spring Valley. They were headed by the Spring Valley Italian Band, and to deceive the negroes into thinking the assembly a peaceful one this band rendered several National apthems. The negroes, as a result, remained in their homes. The Italians fell on them like a lot of Apache Indians. The men were dragged out, clubbed, trampled upon and made the targets for the shotguns, rifles and small arms the mob had brought with them.

The women were insulted, slapped and two of them, while begging for mercy, were shot down and fatally injured.

Sheriff Clark, of Princeton, was telegraphed for and arrived on the ground with a posse, but came too late, as the work had long been done before he arrived. The negroes fled terror-stricken over the surrounding hills and to-night are sleeping under trees and barns, with the exception of a few, whom the farmers are sheltering. Many of the injured are expected to die before morning. No arrests, as yet, have been attempted.

SPRING VALLEY, Ill., Aug. 4.—“The Location,” a patch of some hundred odd company houses near No. 3 shaft, inhabited almost exclusively by negroes, was this morning visited by a vengeful mob of 500 white miners from this city and given a taste of mob violence.

Last night near midnight five colored men held up a white man named Barney Role between this city and Location, and after robbing him of nearly $100, fired three shots into him and left him for dead. Role is the third man shot at Location in the past few weeks.

When the white miners of this city heard of the outrage they assembled on the public square and decided to march in a body to General Manager Dalezill’s house and demand of him the discharge of every colored man in Location. A brass band was secured and the mob repaired to the general manager’s house. He refused to grant what the white miners wanted. They then told him that as he was not disposed to turn the negroes out of town they would take the matter upon themselves, and with that they marched toward No. 3.
By the time the mob arrived at Location most of the negroes, having been notified of the wrath of the whites, had fled to the woods. About a dozen were caught and treated to most violent kicks. Stones were hurled at them and shots fired. Two were shot but not seriously hurt.

The boarding house for colored men at No. 3 was then attacked. All the inmates fled for their lives. The mob ransacked the houses, breaking furniture and committing other uepredations. By noon today every negro had fled. All afternoon a gang of men with pistols and shotguns scoured the woods, hunting for negroes to shoot at.

Sneriff Clark arrived late this afternoon with a band of deputies. No more trouble is anticipated unless the negroes attempt to come back. There is a terrible prejudice nere against them for frequent and bold outrages they are charged with committing. There is much feeling against Dalzell, at whose instance it is alleged they were imported. Everything is quiet tonight, but trouble is expected tomorrow if the negroes go to work.

Later investigation shows that there were more negroes seriously hurt than at first reported. Two persons were fatally injured and twelve others severely wounded.

The rioters were all Italian miners. There has been bad blood between them and the negroes ever since the latter were imported here, and it is asserted that they have been waiting for a good excuse to drive them out. This was furnished by the shooting of last night. Upon reaching the negro village the members of the mob acted as so many fiends. Men were dragged out of their homes, and the women pushed about, slapped and otherwise abused. The Italians poured through the village, firing guns and beating the negroes right and left. As each house was reached the rioters smashed the windows and where doors were locked they broke them down. The interiors were ransacked, the women insulted, and the men dragged forth, clubbed and shot. That there was not a large number of fatalities was no fault of the rioters, as they used every endeavor in their power to kill the men outright. The weapons of the rioters were mostly old rusty guns that had not been used for years, and in addition the men were not skilled in the use of them.

The rioters this evening served notice on the women and children who had not been driven out that they would be given until tomorrow to leave, and if they were not gone they would be snot down in their tracks. Consequently the women have been packing all that is left of their household goods and fleeing over the hills in all directions.

INFLAMMATORY LANGUAGE:

At the secret meeting last night the plan of stopping the men from working was arranged. Over two thousand miners assembled at the lumber yard today at 16 o'clock, and the situation was freely discussed. The coal company was roundly denounced and much inflammatory language used. One speaker said if the murderer was a relative of his he would not stop with the negroes, but would settle it at once and effectively with Manager Dalzell, of the coal company, who, he said, deserved all the blame, as he had brought the negroes here.

After an hour of general discussion a resolution was adopted giving the remnant of negroes left, until 5 o'clock tomorrow evening in which to leave the city and to carry off their effects. If any of the effects are left after that time they will be confiscated and destroyed. A committee was appointed to organize the Italians and see that the instructions were carried out. Another committee of five was appointed to wait upon Manager Dalzell to demand the discharge of all negroes, and to agree to employ no new ones for the present. The committee immediately called at Dalzell's office and stated their grievances, Mr. Dalzell, in reply, said that he had nothing on the subject to state, and that it was a matter he would not discuss. The committee retired without any assurances. All day the streets were crowded with men discussing the situation. Another meeting is called for a later hour to-night, at which time it is believed a continuance of the strike will be ordered.

The foreign element which dominates the situation, declared that no man, either black or white, shall return to work until the coal company agree to discharge every colored man in its employ, and agree to hire no new men of either race until all idle men of Spring Valley are given employment.

The negroes now propose to return to their homes and continue in their employment in the mines of the coal company.

The Spring Valley Coal Company sent its treasurer to Seatonville early this morning, and paid the negroes what was due them up to last Wednesday. The amount due since that time will be paid within a few days.

A CORRESPONDENT'S ESCAPE.

A plan to mob a newspaper correspondent to-day was frustrated only by the latter jumping on a bicycle and riding away. The mob of about two hundred men was composed almost wholly of the men who were engaged in yesterday's riots, and were aggrieved because it had published that none of the guilty had been arrested. The county officials at Princeton, when seen to-night, did not know what steps, if any, would be taken to bring the guilty parties in Spring Valley to terms.

Sheriff Clark said he was discouraged in the matter as not one man was ever convicted in the courts who was arrested a year ago for looting the stores at Spring Valley and Ladd. They were either let off on lack of evidence or technicalities of the court. Stae's Attorney Johnson said he would not be the one to make the complaints. He had personally conducted the cases last year, to no effect, and did not care to go through the same experience again.

The citizens of Spring Valley are in such a state of intimidation that criminal prosecution requiring local witnesses is of no avail.

At the negro at No. 3 shaft pandemonium reigned all night. Crowds of foreigners floated about the streets at all hours discharging fire-arms of various kinds and throwing rocks against the cottages of the negroes.

This was evidently done for the purpose of terrorizing the negroes; in this it was successful.

TEOUBLE ANTICIPATED.

LADD, ILL., Aug. 5.—The foreigners at Spring Valley, under the leadership of the Italians, and the negroes, who have concentrated their forces at Sextonville, are both organizing their men to-day, and as the towns are practically under mob law, a deadly conflict is soon anticipated. The non-English-speaking miners at Spring Valley, to the number of 2,000, had a mass-meeting at the lumber-yard near the Rock Island depot at 10 o'clock this morning, and passed a resolution that no negroes, men, women, or invalids, would be allowed to remain inside the city limits after 5 o'clock tomorrow evening.

Speeches of the most inflammatory nature were made asking the immediate opening of hostilities. The negroes at Sextonville, on the other hand, had a meeting at Union church at 11 o'clock this morning and organized themselves for active service.

Bureau county has repeating Winchester rifles stored in her court-house at Princeton for the protection of the citizens. Should this fail the men will arm themselves with shot-guns or rifles and smaller arms, and make an effort to retain their homes and household goods at Spring Valley. They also adopted a resolution that they would continue to work in the Spring Valley until discharged by the coal company.

As the police and sheriff are making no effort to arrest the rioters, the spirit of lawlessness is on the increase. In addition to the negroes reported killed yesterday, several others are reported missing. Sam Johnson, aged thirty years; Lewis Martin, thirty-five years. Of these, it is believed that the two last are lying dead in the woods surrounding the late negro colony, as two prostrate bodies have been reported.

PEORIA, ILL., Aug. 5.—At a meeting of colored men to-night, twenty-six signed the roll to go to Bureau county to help their brethren. They have arms and ammunition.

Mass Meetings Held by Colored People—Two Refugees' Stories.
CHICAGO, Aug. 6.—Two colored women—Mrs. Mary Stanton and Mrs. Lizzie Dixdee—refugees from Spring Valley, arrived in this city to-night and the reports they give of the treatment of the colored people at that place have inflamed the negroes of Chicago to the highest pitch. Mrs. Stanton is a widow, and since the attack made by the Italians on the colored men at Spring Valley her two sons have disappeared, and she believes that both were killed. Mrs. Dixdee has heard nothing from her husband since that time, and believes him dead. Both women say, in spite of statements to the contrary from Spring Valley, that the reports of the outrages have in no way been exaggerated. They say that the colored women and the children were assaulted by the Italians and brutally beaten, and that it is impossible for any colored woman to walk the streets of the town without being grossly insulted. They declare that all the colored women in Spring Valley were given until 5 o'clock to-night to get out of town, threats of bodily injury being made against those who remained.

The mass meeting of colored men reconvened this evening in Arlington Hall, at Thirty-first street and Indiana avenue. The stories told by the two women inflamed them to the highest pitch, and all manner of violent threats were made against the Italians at Spring Valley. For the first time during the day the idea to move on Spring Valley took definite shape, and committees were appointed to raise funds to secure arms. There was much excitement at the afternoon mass meeting when a telegram was read from Governor Altgeld saying that the officials of Spring Valley and Bureau county had not asked for aid, and if they did it would be promptly sent. This did not suit the colored men at all, and there were loud cries that he was temporizing with them; that he knew the local authorities would not call on him, and the excitement grew so intense that the most warlike language was used. Finally cooler counsel prevailed, and it was decided to give Governor Altgeld time to act.

A delegation called on General Merritt to ask that the United States troops be sent to Spring Valley. They were courteously received by General Merritt, who told the committee that in the event of the failure of the civil authorities to preserve order and protect the colored people of Spring Valley the fact should be communicated to President Cleveland by telegraph, but he did not anticipate that it would be necessary for the national government to take any steps in the matter.

At 1:20 to 1:30 this (Wednesday) morning the meeting was still going on. It was decided, however, to appoint a committee of five, which will visit Spring Valley this morning and investigate matters. The others will follow in a body or remain at home as the telegraph report of the committee suggests.

WAR DECLARED OFF.
Spring Valley Negroes to Be Allowed to Return Home.
THE FOURTEENTH AMENDMENT.
A Mass-Meeting of White Miners Formally Resolves to Recognize It-Fifty Italians Vote No-Work to Be Resumed.
PRINCETON, ILL., August 7. The war on negroes by the Italians of Spring Valley has been declared off. The Spring Valley Coal Company will be permitted to resume operations, and the negroes to return to their homes. This action was taken to-day by a mass-meeting of white miners which assembled in the Court-House square.

About 500 miners was present, the largest part of whom were English-speaking. The Italians and French miners were represented. A resolution was offered providing in the effect that the miners of Spring Valley would recognize the fourteenth amendment to the Constitution of the United States, which guarantees to every person equal liberties, without regard to race, color, or previous condition of servitude, and that the miners of Spring Valley would pledge their earnest support to all officers in the enforcement of the law. After being interpreted, the resolution was put to a vote, and was declared carried by an overwhelming majority. About fifty Italians voted in the negative.

A committee was appointed to wait upon Manager S. M. Dalzell, of the coal company, to inform him of the action of the meeting, and to report that the miners were ready and anxious to return to work in the mines.

Mr. Dalzell was closed with the committee almost one hour. He had had a talk with the miners in the morning, with reference to the proposed meeting. While the resolution adopted was not just what he had wanted, he agreed to recognize it, and to resume operations, probably to-morrow morning.

The Notification Committee, to report the condition of affairs to the colored miners, most of whom are at Seatonville, was also arranged between them. It was composed of the following persons, who went to Seatonville, six miles distant, to night: Manager Dalzell, James O'Connor (president of the State Miners' Federation), Mayor Delmago, and five Spring valley aldermen.

Bush, of Chicago, the representative of the organization of colored people in Chicago. He came in place of Representative John C. Buckner.

The Assistant Adjutant-General had a number of conferences with the city and county authorities, and also a delegation of leading citizens from Princeton, among whom were ey-Congressman Henderson, State-Senator J. W. Templeton, and Editors C. P. Bascom and E. K. Mercer. It was decided to await the development of events before definite action should be decided upon.

Bush, the representative of the Chicago colored people, has a fair complexion, and was thus enabled to talk with persons on both sides without prejudice. He spent the greater part of his time at Seatonville, and investigated the condition of the colored persons reported injured. To-night he said he found the information as to the wounded and clubbing, and the incidents as reported, to be substantially correct. He thought the publication of the mob's doings had in a large measure been the means of bringing the mob's reign to a speedy termination.

He says he has the names of six colored persons at Seatonville whom he found to be badly injured, and the names of two who were slightly injured.

Other injured persons were taken elsewhere. He also found a colored woman in a delicate condition, who had been severely trampled upon.
